A1.justification: Both PDFs describe InfVSR despite the changed title and layout. All supplied text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. V1 ends with references; v2 includes readable Appendices A-G, which are included in this assessment.

before.justification: V1 reports original super-resolution evaluations, runtime measurements, qualitative comparisons and component ablations in Section 4 and Tables 1-4.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds latency profiling, controlled ablations, long-sequence analyses and streaming-method comparisons in its appendices.

M1.justification: V1 keeps visual prompts constant across all chunks; v2 introduces threshold-based reference switching across adjacent chunks. Appendix A.3 also describes scene-cut cache resets and prompt updates. The AR-OSD backbone, rolling cache, principal losses and two-stage training design remain.

E1.justification: Both use REDS for training and UDM10, SPMCS, MVSR4x, VideoLQ and MovieLQ for evaluation. Additional resolution and sequence-length profiling extends experimental settings within the same task. Appendix A.3 describes multi-shot handling but supplies no corresponding evaluation results.

E2.justification: Appendix E adds evaluated comparisons against DLoraL and FlashVSR on UDM10 and VideoLQ, substantially extending comparison to relevant streaming approaches. DLoraL was only discussed in v1. The original comparator sets remain; Stream-DiffVSR is discussed but explicitly not evaluated.

E3.justification: The original training settings, scaling factor and benchmark metrics remain. New protocols include varying cache length with chunk size fixed, comparing causal and full attention across lengths and 720p/1080p resolutions, and evaluating five consecutive 200-frame MovieLQ intervals. These materially extend controlled and long-horizon evaluation without establishing reruns of the original experiments.

E4.justification: Table 4d adds removal of the temporal loss. Appendix D adds comparison with optical-flow supervision, isolated cache-length sensitivity, causal versus full-attention scaling, and temporal error-accumulation analysis. These directly test design choices and long-sequence reliability beyond v1's retained ablations.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports repeated-run counts, evaluation seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations or significance tests. The additional result tables retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1-2, original Table 3 timings and retained Table 4 values are unchanged. V2 adds substantial latency, scaling, ablation, segment-wise and comparator results. For example, Table 10 reports higher UDM10 DOVER for FlashVSR than InfVSR (0.7953 versus 0.7826), but lower warping error for InfVSR (1.95 versus 2.47). These are new comparisons, not improved scores for the retained InfVSR evaluation.

T1.justification: Equations 1-6 retain the mathematical formulation; the gradient-subscript correction clarifies notation. Appendix formulas explain existing VBench metrics and a cited comparison loss. The error-accumulation discussion supplies intuition, without adding formal assumptions, derivations or proofs.

C1.justification: The introduction and related work qualify the priority claim from 'first' to 'among the first' and emphasize consistency-driven streaming. The principal claims about AR-OSD, unbounded-length processing, MovieLQ, semantic consistency and up to 58-fold acceleration remain.

C2.justification: Appendix D attributes flow-loss failure to small training windows and argues that LR conditioning limits error accumulation. Appendix F adds substantive limitations concerning training scale, architectural redundancy and VAE/DiT priors. Appendix A also clarifies the single-shot experimental boundary and discusses scene-transition handling.

D1.justification: V2 adds Stage-II pseudocode, regularizer updates and timestep sampling, causal-VAE caching and streaming execution details, MovieLQ's ten-clip count, and metric implementations. Its access statement changes from forthcoming code to available code and models. Some ambiguity remains: Appendix A.2 describes overlapping chunks while Section 3.1 specifies non-overlapping chunks.

R1.justification: V2 updates positioning around concurrent FlashVSR and Stream-DiffVSR, qualifies priority, removes the dedicated one-step-diffusion survey and adds contextual references. The principal relationship to T2V priors and autoregressive generation remains. Publication and bibliographic corrections to retained works are not additional research coverage.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper, substantially rewrites the introduction around three consistency-focused themes, revises method explanations and removes the standalone one-step-diffusion discussion. It also introduces an organized appendix narrative and impact and acknowledgment sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 is replaced, the separate patch-supervision illustration is removed, and new streaming, dataset and comparison displays are added. V1 Figures 4-6 survive as v2 Figures 3-5. Table 3 gains columns, Table 4 gains a row, and Tables 5-10 are new.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves support for the central streaming claims: Appendices A-B explain execution and training, D tests scaling and long-video degradation, and E adds directly relevant streaming competitors with visible metric trade-offs. Concrete limitations further improve transparency. These address important gaps in v1's validation and reproducibility despite unchanged headline scores. Conflicting overlap descriptions and insufficiently reconciled efficiency settings remain, but the added evidence and documentation provide a clear overall gain.
